title: How Dogs Could Help Japan Save $1 Billion a Year
paragraphs: Dogs are often called "man's best friend." They give us company, love and a reason to get outside for a walk.
But could they also help save Japan almost $1 billion a year?
A new study suggests that increasing dog ownership among older people could help Japan reduce its long-term care costs.
Researchers believe dogs may help lower the risk of their owners getting dementia.

The study followed over 11,000 people in Tokyo aged 65 to 84 for seven-and-a-half years. During that time, among people who never owned dogs, 18% developed dementia-related care needs. Among dog owners, that fell to 13%.
Caring for people with dementia is expensive. So if owning a dog helps lower the risk of dementia, it could save the Japanese government a lot of money.

Nine percent of people in the study owned dogs. The researchers estimate that if dog ownership among older people across Japan increased to 13%, the country could save 150 billion yen — almost $1 billion — each year in long-term care costs.
The study couldn't prove that owning a dog prevents dementia. But there are reasons why having a dog might help.

Walking a dog can help owners stay active and give them more ways to meet other people. Dogs also give their owners company and a daily routine. And previous research suggests these things can help lower the risk of dementia.
But owning a dog as an older person isn't always easy. What if an owner becomes ill or goes into the hospital? Who will care for the dog?
The study's researchers say Japan needs more support for older dog owners, so they can enjoy life with their pets knowing someone will help care for them if needed.
